Buses are scheduled so the average gap between arrivals is exactly 10 minutes, but the actual gaps vary in length rather than all being equal. If you arrive at the bus stop at a uniformly random moment, is your average wait for the next bus more than, equal to, or less than 5 minutes?
choices: More than 5 minutes — a random arrival is more likely to land inside one of the longer gaps, oversampling them
Exactly 5 minutes, since that's half the average gap
It cannot be determined without knowing the exact gap lengths
Less than 5 minutes, since a bus is equally likely to have just left as to be due soon

questions.q: Die A has faces {4,4,4,4,0,0}. Die B has faces {3,3,3,3,3,3}. Die C has faces {6,6,2,2,2,2}. Each pair is rolled against each other many times (higher face wins). Die A beats Die B more often, and Die B beats Die C more often. Does Die A necessarily beat Die C more often too?
choices: Yes — if A beats B and B beats C, A must beat C by transitivity
No such A, B, C can exist with these win patterns
No — C actually beats A more often, since 'beats more often' is not transitive for dice
It's a tie — A and C each win exactly half the rolls

questions.q: Which weighs more: one kilogram of feathers, or one kilogram of steel?
choices: They weigh exactly the same — a kilogram is a kilogram regardless of material
The steel — metal is denser so it's heavier
It depends on the current gravity at the location
The feathers — they take up more space so there's 'more' of them

questions.q: Among patients admitted to a hospital, doctors notice that having Disease A makes a patient statistically LESS likely to also have Disease B. Yet in the general population, Disease A and Disease B are completely independent — having one tells you nothing about your chances of having the other. Both findings are correct and there is no data error. How is this possible?
choices: The sample of admitted patients is too small for the correlation to mean anything
Two truly independent events can never show any correlation in any subgroup, so the hospital's data must be wrong
Disease A must secretly provide partial immunity to Disease B

Being admitted to the hospital typically requires being sick with A, B, or something else; conditioning on admission alone can create a spurious negative association between two otherwise-independent conditions (Berkson's paradox)

In a single round of the Ultimatum Game, Player A is given $100 and proposes how to split it with Player B. Player B can only accept (both keep their share) or reject (both get nothing) — there are no further rounds. Assuming both players are purely rational and self-interested, caring only about maximizing their own money, and the split can be made in $1 increments, what split should Player A propose?
choices: It cannot be determined without knowing Player B's personal values
A 50/50 split, since it's the fairest outcome
Keep all $100 and give Player B nothing
Give Player B $1 and keep $99, the smallest offer B should still accept

questions.q: You have two glasses holding exactly equal volumes of liquid — one full of wine, one full of water. You take a spoonful of wine from the wine glass and stir it into the water glass. Then, without measuring, you take a spoonful of the now-mixed liquid from the water glass and stir it back into the wine glass, so both glasses once again hold equal volumes. Is there now more water in the wine glass, or more wine in the water glass?
choices: More water in the wine glass than wine in the water glass
More wine in the water glass than water in the wine glass
Exactly the same amount either way, regardless of how thoroughly it was mixed
It cannot be determined without knowing the size of the spoon

questions.q: A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across a river one item at a time (plus himself). Left alone, the wolf eats the goat, and the goat eats the cabbage. What is the minimum number of river crossings required?
Which is larger: the number of distinct ways to shuffle a standard 52-card deck (52!), or the number of atoms on Earth (roughly 10^50)?
choices: It's impossible to meaningfully compare a permutation count to a physical count
They are roughly equal, both around 10^50
The number of atoms on Earth — a mere 52 cards can't compete with atoms
The number of ways to shuffle a deck of cards (52!) — it vastly exceeds the number of atoms on Earth

questions.q: Three voters rank three candidates A, B, and C as follows — Voter 1: A > B > C. Voter 2: B > C > A. Voter 3: C > A > B. In pairwise majority votes, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A, each by 2 votes to 1 — so the group's collective preference cycles even though every individual voter's own ranking is perfectly transitive. What is this phenomenon called?
